title: Salem Possessed: The Social Origins of Witchcraft
author: Paul Boyer and Stephen Nissenbaum
subject_focus: Community social origins of the 1692 Salem witchcraft crisis, arguing that accusations mapped onto pre-existing factional divisions between Salem Village's subsistence agricultural community and Salem Town's commercial interests.
summary: Boyer and Nissenbaum's Salem Possessed is the founding work of the social-origins approach to the Salem crisis. Drawing on tax records, church membership lists, land records, and petition signatures, Boyer and Nissenbaum constructed a social geography of Salem Village's accusation patterns and demonstrated that the line between accusers and accused tracked closely with a pre-existing factional division in the village: accusers were predominantly from the anti-commercial, subsistence-agricultural, western part of Salem Village centered on the Putnam family; accused were predominantly from the more commercially oriented, market-integrated, eastern part associated with Salem Town and Porter family interests. The authors argued that witchcraft accusation provided a socially available mechanism for processing the profound anxieties generated by Salem Village's conflict-ridden experience of early capitalist transformation — the loss of the subsistence community ideal in the face of commercial integration.
scholarly_significance:
Salem Possessed is one of the most influential works in American colonial social history and the foundational work for the social-community-conflict approach to Salem. Its significance is the demonstration that witch accusation patterns were not random but structured — that the geography of accusation in Salem Village revealed underlying social divisions that predated the crisis and gave it its specific shape.

  The book's major contribution was methodological: the use of quantitative social-historical analysis (tax records, land ownership maps, petition signatures) to reconstruct the social geography of accusation. Subsequent Salem scholarship has both built on and contested Boyer and Nissenbaum: Karlsen's property-inheritance analysis (1987) and Norton's frontier-trauma thesis (2002) offer complementary or alternative explanations that Boyer and Nissenbaum's community-conflict framework does not fully address. Historiographical consensus treats the Boyer-Nissenbaum model as partially correct — the factional division was real and mattered — but insufficient as a complete explanation for the scale and character of the crisis.

key_arguments.claim: The geography of accusation in Salem Village was not random but tracked a pre-existing factional division between subsistence-agricultural (Putnam-dominated, western) and commercially-oriented (Porter-connected, eastern) community interests — accusers predominantly from one side, accused predominantly from the other.

key_arguments.concept: Early capitalist anxiety as cultural context
key_arguments.claim: The Salem crisis expressed anxiety generated by Salem Village's experience of early capitalist transformation — the erosion of the subsistence community ideal in favor of market integration — for which witchcraft accusation provided a culturally available processing mechanism.

relation_to_database: Boyer and Nissenbaum are referenced in the salem-1692-trials trial_event entry, the property-holding-women persecuted group entry, and in the accused_person entries for Bridget Bishop, Rebecca Nurse, Sarah Good, and Giles Corey.
scholarly_disagreement: The Boyer-Nissenbaum factional map has been contested by subsequent scholars who find exceptions to the pattern and question whether the factional division was as determinative as they argue. Norton's frontier thesis, Karlsen's property analysis, and Bernard Rosenthal's evidentiary skepticism represent alternative or supplementary frameworks. The degree to which early capitalism versus specific community-level conflicts versus regional trauma context explains Salem remains unsettled.
source_method: Published text, Harvard University Press 1974; primary sources: Essex County Court records, Salem Village tax and church records
